name: C4 L2 Containers - private container app
title: Privately accessible container app
subtitle: C4 level 2: Containers
description: Inside one environment's resource group: users on the corporate network reach the internal load balancer of the Container Apps environment through hub peering; the Private DNS zone, linked to the spoke and the hub, resolves the app name. Built-in authentication signs them in with Entra ID before any request reaches the web application, which is generic: any image that serves HTTP on port 8000 and answers /healthz. It pulls its image from the registry with a managed identity, sends traces, requests and exceptions to Application Insights, and alerts fire through the Action Group. Nothing is reachable from the internet.

nodes.label: Health checks and alerts: what they watch and why
items: Probes:
GET /healthz on port 8000, sent by the Container Apps platform from inside the environment, as both the liveness and the readiness probe. The request never leaves the private network.
Why the platform probes, not a web test:
the app has no public address, so Azure's internet availability tests cannot reach it from any region.
Why /healthz:
it is the only path excluded from sign-in (authConfigs excludedPaths), so the platform can call it without a token. Every other path redirects to Entra ID.
What happens on failure:
a failed liveness probe restarts the container; a failed readiness probe takes the replica out of traffic.
Alerts:
severity 2 when the container restarts at all within 15 minutes, and severity 2 when more than 5 requests return 5xx within 15 minutes. Both are checked every 5 minutes and email the Action Group.
Traces:
when APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING is set, the app sends OpenTelemetry traces, requests, dependencies, exceptions and logs to Application Insights.
Does not prove:

that users can reach the app over the hub and corporate DNS, or that sign-in works (nothing tests from outside the environment). A replica stuck as not ready raises no alert, because it is not restarted and returns no 5xx.

nodes.label: How users reach the app, and how it reports back
items: ## What happens
A user opens the app's internal address from the corporate network; the hub and private DNS take them straight to it, never over the internet
Microsoft Entra ID checks that they belong to an allowed group before the app sees the request
Azure checks every few seconds that the app is alive and restarts it if it is not
The app records what it did and any errors in Azure monitoring; restarts and bursts of errors email the team
## Why we do it this way
The app is for internal users only, so it has no public address at all
Sign-in is handled by Azure, so the app never sees passwords
Any team can bring its own app: it only has to answer on port 8000 and at /healthz

nodes.label: What to keep in mind
items: Hub dependency:
users reach the app only once the platform team completes the hub side (peering, routing and corporate DNS for the environment domain). Agree it before the first apply.
Public egress:

image pulls and telemetry go to public Azure endpoints (Basic registry, no Monitor Private Link), protected by identity and keys. If policy requires private-only traffic, move to a Premium registry and a Monitor Private Link Scope.
Sign-in secret:
it rotates every 180 days, but only on the next apply. An environment left unapplied for about 210 days stops signing users in.
Zones and replicas:
uat and prod run 2 replicas spread across availability zones (zone_redundancy_enabled, fixed at creation). dev and qa run 1 replica in one zone, so a crash there is a short outage.
Request limit:
ingress ends requests after 240 seconds, and the app server may cut them sooner (the example uses a 120 s gunicorn timeout).
Cost:

about $35 a month in dev and qa and $67 in uat and prod when mostly idle (up to $109 and $219 if busy all month), at West Europe list prices. Compute is most of it; the Basic registry is $5, or $51 as Premium for zone redundancy. A budget warns at 80 % actual and 100 % forecast.

nodes.label: Why pick this design, and its trade-offs
items: Container Apps, not App Service:

runs any image with no App Service plan to size. An internal environment gives private ingress without a separate private endpoint. Trade-off: less control over the runtime than App Service plans; the environment needs its own /27 subnet.
Container Apps, not AKS:
no cluster to run, patch or secure for one small web app. Trade-off: no custom sidecars, operators or cluster add-ons.
Internal load balancer only:
every user is internal, so there is no internet surface to defend. The public variant, with Front Door and WAF, is a separate template. Trade-off: no one off the corporate network can reach it.
Zone-redundant in uat and prod, not everywhere:
prod keeps serving through a zone failure and uat rehearses it; dev and qa do not need it. Trade-off: fixed at creation, and the second always-on replica costs about $32 a month.
Built-in sign-in, not in-app code:
one Entra setup works for any language, Entra itself enforces the allowed groups, and the app stays generic. Trade-off: fine-grained roles still need code that reads the claims.
Managed identity, not registry passwords:
the admin user is off, so there are no credentials to store or rotate. Trade-off: the pipeline still needs AcrPush through its own service connection.
Basic registry, not Premium:
a private registry needs Premium, which a small workload does not justify. Revisit if policy requires private endpoints. Trade-off: the registry keeps a public endpoint and no geo-replication.
No storage account:
the app is stateless. Add Blob storage only when it must keep files or run longer than 240 seconds. Trade-off: nothing survives a restart.
